episode.title: Cariboo Signals - Repair Culture & Practical Tech
episode.description:
Riley and Casey explore technology and society in rural communities. Today's focus: Repair Culture & Practical Tech.

THIS WEEK WE'RE ASKING: Is staying put a virtue or a failure of nerve?

NEWS ROUNDUP: We break down Williams Lake non-profit helping reduce cat overpopulation with spaying, neutering and Quesnel City Council seeks provincial help to try to get QRP up and running again, plus 12 more stories, and explore what these developments mean for communities like ours.

RURAL CONNECTIONS: Is a small independent repair shop's ability to service vehicles and maintain its systems something it truly owns, or access it rents and must defend alone? Topics include: Manufacturer subscription costs and diagnostic software pricing for independent shops, Reliability and sourcing of U.S. repair cost estimates versus local Cariboo conditions, Cybersecurity risks and safety arguments used by automakers against independent repair access, Right-to-repair legislation and federal executive actions, including the stalled bill and June memo, Succession planning and owner-held records as protection against lock-in.

Hosts: Riley (Tech optimist with an engineering background) and Casey (Community-first skeptic of tech promises).

COMMUNITY SPOTLIGHT: Williams Lake Women's Centre

articles.title: [Adafruit Blog] It’s time we demand the right to repair our cars
articles.summary: Kyle Wiens has written up Closing Shop at iFixit News, a new report on automotive software locks written with Nathan Proctor of U.S. PIRG Education Fund and Kevin O’Reilly of FULU. Automakers are putt...

discussion.central_question: Is a small independent repair shop's ability to service vehicles and maintain its systems something it truly owns, or access it rents and must defend alone?
discussion.riley_position: The subscription and software costs are a real lock-in, but shops can make deliberate, budget-conscious choices about which makes to serve, and the fight is better won through open diagnostic access rules and owner-held records than through despair.
riley_key_evidence: The Closing Shop report (iFixit, U.S. PIRG Education Fund, FULU Foundation) puts annual cost for one shop working on five manufacturers' cars at $15,878 before any repair revenue.
Diagnosing an electrical fault in a Ford F-150 taillight costs $2,178 once repair information, diagnostic software, and an adapter kit are added.

Mechanics spend a median of 1.25 hours per repair just getting through manufacturer software, and a June Trump administration 'freedom to fix' memo exists though critics say it covers emissions parts rather than the software paywall.
discussion.casey_position: The access is rented and the owner carries the costs and risks alone, since the numbers are U.S.-based, the headline estimates rest on thin evidence, and rules will arrive too late for shops already locked into subscriptions.
casey_key_evidence: The $12 billion headline estimate draws on 83 million mechanic hours and a $140 labour rate, but a critical read in The Auto Wire notes the survey base was only 28 responses.
WIRED reports a new wave of AI penetration-testing tools since late August hitting companies, government agencies, and banks, which small shops with a single owner-run server are exposed to.
Ford's Jim Farley has said letting owners repair new vehicles at home 'would put people's lives at risk,' while automakers cite cybersecurity and counterfeit-parts concerns.
discussion.resolution: They did not fully agree. Riley conceded that the Williams Lake and Quesnel pricing is unverified and likely similar rather than confirmed, and Casey conceded the records are the cheapest safeguard. They left open who decides when a shop moves from choosing to stay to making do, agreeing only on practical steps like writing down subscriptions, passwords, and reset steps and testing the network.

research.block:
PRE-RESEARCHED INSIGHTS FOR THE DEEP DIVE

RESEARCH QUESTION: Are the Closing Shop report's headline numbers ($15,878 a year per mechanic, $12 billion total) holding up, and what is the automakers' counter-case?

Findings: The $15,878 figure is repeated across iFixit, the FULU Foundation, PIRG and Adafruit. It is a subscription-cost estimate for one shop servicing cars from five manufacturers, paid before any repair revenue comes in. The report is a joint project of the Repair.org coalition, authored by U.S. PIRG Education Fund, iFixit and FULU Foundation. Its other key finding is that mechanics spend a median of 1.25 hours per repair navigating manufacturer software. The report's estimate of 83 million mechanic hours a year, equal to about 42,000 full-time technicians, is the basis for the $12 billion cost figure. A critical read in The Auto Wire argues the $12 billion rests on a thin survey base (28 answers) and a $140 labor-rate assumption, so the price list is the strongest evidence and the aggregate is the most assailable. Automakers' stated position is safety and security: Ford's Jim Farley has said that letting owners repair a new vehicle at home "would put people's lives at risk." Automakers and dealers say they support repair access but raise cybersecurity and counterfeit-parts concerns. Federal right-to-repair legislation remains stalled as of 2026. In June 2026 the Trump administration issued a "freedom to fix" memo that, according to critics, covers only emissions parts and not the broader software-paywall problem. Reuters reported that the White House met with the auto industry in June 2026 over the debate.

Suggested angle: Riley can argue the price list is concrete proof that a repair toll road now exists, and that open diagnostic data is the practical fix, the same way independent Linux and open hardware communities solved lock-in elsewhere. Casey should press on the aggregate: a $12 billion headline built on 28 survey responses and an assumed labor rate deserves scrutiny, and the safety/cybersecurity objection is not trivial for a car's braking or driver-assistance systems. The strongest exchange is over who should hold the keys to diagnostic access (owners, independent shops, or regulators with security certification), not whether repair matters. Riley's best counter is that the safety argument is currently used to justify paywalls that the same manufacturers already share with franchised dealers.

roundup.opening_frame: A day of local council business and small-town notices, then a run of stories about who gets to fix, keep and keep running the things people depend on.

stories.point: WL Kitty Spay, a non-profit founded just over two years ago, held its first Pet Vendor Market at Cariboo Corner on Nov. 21, and has helped fund spaying or neutering for more than 170 cats.

Quesnel City Council unanimously endorsed a letter asking the Ministers of Forests and BC Hydro to meet about the indefinite curtailment at Quesnel River Pulp, which Millar Western blamed on weak demand and tariffs on Chinese exports.
The Cariboo-Chilcotin School District board elected Mike Franklin of Zone 6 as chair and Melissa Coates of Zone 4 as vice-chair.
70 Mile House has a Christmas craft fair on Nov. 28, monthly pancake breakfasts are back, and the community hall's Christmas dinner waits on hall work being finished.
An air quality warning for coarse particulate matter was issued Nov. 24 for the North Cariboo, including Quesnel, with advice to cut strenuous outdoor activity and stay in filtered air.
Low-tech Magazine runs on a solar-powered website that sometimes goes offline, and its book collection is now available in epub.

A repair guide for the Elegoo Saturn 4 Ultra 16K says an LCD connection error may be a slipped ribbon cable or mismatched firmware, checkable in 7 screws, before buying the $129.99 screen that takes 58 screws to fit.
stories.bridge_to_next: Repair as a topic: from a hobby printer that can be fixed cheaply to a wheelchair whose repair has become slow.

stories.point: Two private equity-backed companies now dominate the U.S. wheelchair market, and as they buy local repair shops, waits for repairs can stretch to weeks or months with dangerous health consequences.

A string of outages at JPMorgan Chase, the FAA and Microsoft over five days left Americans unable to email, fly or reach their accounts, and one adviser says out-of-date systems under upgrade are a likelier cause than attackers. This is a U.S. matter, not ours to vote on, but worth watching for precedent.
Munich-based RECNAS is preparing a crowdfunding campaign for AGP4SATA, a board that turns old AGP-slot PCs into four-bay NAS machines, and says even a Pentium 4 build can idle below 20W.
stories.bridge_to_next: Old hardware kept working: from an old PC turned into storage to a 1986 terminal being pieced back together.

stories.point: A blog post documents a PC Shadow PCT 5000 green-screen terminal that arrived with 8-inch floppies, is in decent shape apart from failing RIFA capacitors, and was likely built to work with the MultiLink multi-user DOS package.
Earlier this week: Ericsson is developing mobile network technology that detects and tracks drones, with commercial trials planned for 2027 and wider deployment in 2028.
stories.bridge_to_next: Drones as a topic: from tracking drones through the phone network to drones that work on power lines.

stories.point: Nomadic's 4kg drones land on live 420 kV power lines, recharge from the magnetic field, and have logged 20,000 hours inspecting European and US grids for bottlenecks.
A hacker stopped a LiftMaster MyQ Home Bridge garage door controller from rebooting when offline by extracting its encryption key and running a dummy MQTT server.
stories.bridge_to_next: Devices tied to a maker's servers and data: from a garage opener that wants its maker's cloud to a fitness app that charges to export your own records.

stories.point: MyFitnessPal only lets users export their data with a premium subscription, so one user wrote a free Chrome extension to export it and shared it.
Koshiro Robot built a dozen robot actuator motors, drivers and control firmware almost entirely DIY, all published openly.
ArchDaily says shipping container buildings are cheap and durable but constrained by their 2.44m width and thermal conductivity, and need careful planning.
USB-C cables look alike but differ in data and power capability, because the standard only fixes the connector shape, so a tester had to check dozens of cables.

roundup.handoff: Who holds the keys to the things people fix and keep running: the owner, the maker, or whoever sells the diagnostic access.

deep_dive.central_question: When a small-town mechanic or tinkerer builds their own shop and network rather than leaving for a city job, is the independence they get something they own, or access they rent from manufacturers and have to defend alone?
deep_dive.riley_holds: Riley holds that a tradesperson who stays and builds a shop is making a real choice, and that access can be won back through rules and open tools.
deep_dive.casey_holds: Casey holds that a shop kept going on subscriptions and an exposed network may be making do rather than self-reliance, because the keys sit with others.

beats.claim: The question gets asked plainly here: is staying and running your own shop a virtue or a failure of nerve? The first test is cost, because a mechanic who stays and fixes cars is renting the ability to do so from the manufacturers.
beats.evidence: Adafruit Blog on the iFixit report Closing Shop, written with U.S. PIRG Education Fund and FULU: one mechanic needs $15,878 a year in subscriptions to work on cars from five major manufacturers, and diagnosing a Ford F-150 taillight fault costs $2,178 in repair information, software and an adapter kit.
beats.pushback: Riley: the $15,878 figure covers five manufacturers, so a shop that picks its makes pays less, and choosing what to serve is itself an act of independence.
beats.leads_to_next: If cost is a choice the shop can manage, the next question is whether the shop's own tools, such as a server or network, are actually under its owner's control.

beats.claim: A homelab or shop network that the owner built is only as independent as its security, and the owner is their own security staff.
beats.evidence: WIRED on Artex: since around the end of August, companies, agencies and banks worldwide have been hit by AI penetration-testing harnesses that scan targets and force their way into poorly secured networks, letting newbie hackers wage attacks via chatbot prompts.
beats.pushback: Riley: WIRED says many of these setups mimic legitimate defensive penetration testing, so the same methods are available to a careful owner to test their own network.
beats.leads_to_next: Casey's point stands that self-reliance carries a duty, so the question becomes whether independence depends on the individual's nerve or on rules that give them access.

beats.claim: The independence that staying promises becomes real only when the law frees the access, which shifts the question from nerve to policy.
beats.evidence: Adafruit Blog: the iFixit report says automakers are putting ordinary repairs behind software locks that mechanics must subscribe to, and the post's headline is a call to demand the right to repair cars.
beats.pushback: Casey: the headline is a demand, not a result. The report documents locks that exist now, and a shop owner cannot plan a decade of staying on a law that has not passed.
beats.leads_to_next: If the rules are still being fought for, the test has to be applied to a real place where someone is staying now.

beats.claim: In the Cariboo, the independent garage is the clearest test: a Williams Lake or Quesnel shop serving local pickups stays by choice only if it controls its diagnostics, data and network, and otherwise it is making do.
beats.evidence: Draws on the iFixit figures from the Adafruit Blog item on subscription costs per manufacturer and the WIRED report on attacks on poorly secured networks, applied to a shop that serves several makes of truck.
beats.pushback: Riley: a shop that serves ranch and logging trucks locally can choose to specialise in the makes it can afford to support, so staying can still be deliberate.
beats.leads_to_next: This points to what a shop must own outright for staying to count as self-reliance, which sets up the landing.

set_aside: The Tyee on a BC public developer building a housing asset portfolio, which does not bear on repair or self-reliance in the material provided
WIRED on the lawsuit against xAI over Grok-edited images, which is about image abuse and not about staying put or self-reliance
deep_dive.cariboo_beat: Beat 4: a Williams Lake or Quesnel independent garage serving ranch and logging trucks stands in for the question, asking what that shop owns outright versus rents.
deep_dive.landing: Held open: which parts of a shop must its owner hold outright, diagnostic access, the repair records or the network, before staying counts as self-reliance rather than making do, and who decides when that line is crossed.
